threads.body: [General] `registerFromSeedNodes` only succeeds for sets previously returned by the instrumented `ConnectionStringUtil`. The public `Cluster.connect(Set<SeedNode>, ...)` and `AsyncCluster.connect(Set<SeedNode>, ...)` paths pass the caller's set directly, so on 3.1–3.5 this lookup returns null and the stable server attributes are omitted, contrary to the PR's advertised seed-node support. Please derive a target from an uncached `SeedNode` set (while preferring the cached original for DNS-SRV) and cover a direct seed-set connection path.

replies.body:
Addressed in fd3245d002b6b29b5a0a2270d5eae35b78552b6e.

Analysis: Direct `SeedNode` connections bypass `ConnectionStringUtil`, so the core registration has no cached parsed target. The registration now uses the cached target first to preserve the original DNS-SRV host. It otherwise builds a target from each seed's address and key-value port. The 3.1 integration test now connects through the direct seed-set API, so its stable semantic convention assertions cover this path.

Upsides: Direct `Cluster.connect(Set<SeedNode>, ...)` and `AsyncCluster.connect(Set<SeedNode>, ...)` calls now emit the configured server address and port. Connection-string calls still retain the original DNS-SRV host.

Downsides: Multi-seed target ordering follows the iteration order of the caller's set.

threads.body: [General] On current 3.x clients, `Core.create(..., Set<SeedNode>)` converts the set to a synthetic `ConnectionString` by iterating the set before invoking this constructor. Treating every parsed connection string as original input therefore preserves arbitrary set iteration order, so equivalent direct seed sets can emit different multi-endpoint `server.address` values instead of the deterministic value promised by this PR. Capture/overwrite the target at the `Core.create(..., Set)` boundary using the sorted direct-seed representation (while retaining order only for actual connection-string input), and cover this through the latest-deps path.

replies.body:
Addressed in e7e0ea2fac080045487d6be3aa8c263ed8fb3076.

Analysis: Current Couchbase clients convert direct seed sets to parsed connection strings before constructing Core. Constructor advice preserves that synthetic order. Exit advice on the direct-seed Core factory now overwrites the target with the sorted seed-set representation. A latest-dependency test calls that factory with reverse-ordered seeds and checks the stored target.

Upsides: Direct seed sets now produce a stable server.address while real connection strings still retain their configured order. The latest client path has regression coverage.

Downsides: The latest-dependency test creates and shuts down one extra Core instance.

threads.body: [General] This adds every KV/manager occurrence, not every distinct endpoint promised by the PR. `SeedNode` equality includes both optional ports, so a valid set can contain `(node, kv=11210, manager=8091)` and `(node, kv=11210, manager=8092)`; this code emits `node:11210` twice. Deduplicate host/port pairs in this direct-seed fallback while leaving original connection-string duplicates intact.

replies.body:
Addressed in 00e6bdde94e3cd0ec47e0ccb50067c61e70d252f.

Analysis: Distinct SeedNode values can share one host and port when their other port differs. The direct-seed target builder now tracks ports by address and adds each endpoint once. Connection-string parsing still uses the order-preserving builder directly, so configured duplicates remain intact.

Upsides: Direct seed targets now contain every distinct endpoint exactly once. Unit and latest-client tests cover duplicate KV endpoints with different manager ports.

Downsides: Direct seed target creation allocates a small map and set to track seen endpoints.

threads.body: [General] `isValidDnsSrv()` only means this is a single-host DNS-SRV candidate; Couchbase additionally requires `CoreEnvironment.ioConfig().dnsSrvEnabled()`. With DNS SRV disabled, the client uses this as a direct seed, but this branch still reports a `couchbase(s)://` discovery identity. Thread the actual DNS-SRV-enabled flag from the core/environment advice into target parsing and use the direct endpoint representation when it is false.

replies.body:
Addressed in ae65417d37f289c4d751bf4109eb3890e80e6126.

Analysis: `ConnectionString.isValidDnsSrv()` identifies a candidate, while `IoConfig.dnsSrvEnabled()` decides whether Couchbase performs DNS SRV discovery. The core advice now passes that setting into connection-string parsing. The seed-node carrier path also converts a stored discovery target to its direct endpoint form when the environment disables DNS SRV.

Upsides: `server.address` and the stable span name now match the endpoint mode Couchbase uses. Both direct core construction and the older seed-node construction path use the environment setting.

Downsides: The parser keeps compatibility overloads that assume DNS SRV is enabled for callers that do not have a `CoreEnvironment`.

threads.body: [General] Couchbase 3.12.2's `DATABASE` convention reports the collection hook as `couchbase.collection.name`. This condition recognizes only the generic key and Couchbase's V0 key, so current stable-mode KV spans miss `_default` and fall back to the bucket or server in their name. Accept the current V1 hook key as well.

replies.body:
Addressed in e9146852d463ff38b10e313f81798c96bfd54072.

Analysis: Couchbase 3.12.2 maps its V1 collection hook to `couchbase.collection.name`, while V0 maps statements to `db.statement`. The bridge now recognizes the V1 collection key and reserves query-summary naming for the real `db.query.summary` key.

Upsides: Stable KV spans use the collection in their names. Query text and its literals no longer become high-cardinality span names.

Downsides: V0 query spans without a real summary now fall back to the namespace, server target, or operation.

threads.body: [General] Treating `db.statement` as `db.query.summary` puts raw query text into the span name. Couchbase maps its V0 statement hook to `db.statement` and passes query statements through it; unlike a query summary, this is high-cardinality and can contain literals. Remove this fallback so the documented collection/namespace/server precedence applies when no real summary exists.

threads.body: This parsing assumes the Testcontainers connection string always contains exactly one host and an explicit trailing port, and that `lastIndexOf(':')` separates host/port (which won’t hold for IPv6 literals or DNS-SRV style identities). Consider extracting the host/port via Couchbase’s `ConnectionString` API (or another structured parser) to make the test resilient if Testcontainers changes formatting or runs under different networking setups.

replies.body:
Addressed in 726a5f899ea156b111ec59fb3d122ec85d08d8b1.

Analysis: Both tests split the Testcontainers connection string at its last colon. That treats an IPv6 colon as a host and port separator. The tests now use Couchbase's `ConnectionString` parser and read the parsed seed host and port.

Upsides: The setup and expected attributes use the same structured host and port values that Couchbase reads. IPv6 literals no longer break the test parser.

Downsides: The tests still use the first seed because each Testcontainers instance exposes one Couchbase server.

threads.body: The test derives `server.address` / `server.port` by substringing the connection string, which is brittle (e.g., DNS-SRV style strings without explicit ports, IPv6 literals with multiple ':', or connection strings with additional components). Using Couchbase’s `ConnectionString.create(connectionString)` (or another structured parser) to read hosts/ports would make the test more robust and reduce the chance of CI flakes on different environments.

threads.body: Deduplication in `portsByAddress` keys on the raw `port` value, which treats ‘no port (0)’ and an explicitly configured scheme-default port (e.g., 11210 / 11207) as distinct. Depending on how `DbServerTarget` renders endpoints, this can produce duplicate rendered endpoints for the same host (e.g., when one `SeedNode` has no KV port and another explicitly sets the default). Consider normalizing the port used for deduplication so that missing ports and explicit default ports are treated equivalently (e.g., map `port == 0` and `port == defaultPort` to a single canonical value), while still passing `-1` to `addEndpoint()` for the ‘missing’ case.

replies.body:
Addressed in 4160f486cc39c6e05853971c3a05fa6628c6965a.

Analysis: `DbServerTargetBuilder` resolves a missing port to the scheme default. The seed-node deduplication ran before that resolution, so a missing port and an explicit default port survived as two endpoints. The deduplication key now uses the effective default port while preserving the original value passed to the builder.

Upsides: Equivalent seed-node forms render once. Non-default ports remain distinct, and the builder still knows whether the client configured a port explicitly.

Downsides: No material downside identified.

threads.body: `emitStableDatabaseSemconv()` is evaluated for every attribute call on the hot path. Since the stability mode is effectively process-wide configuration, consider evaluating it once (e.g., in the span wrapper constructor) and storing it in a boolean field to avoid repeated checks during high-volume attribute recording.

replies.body:
No code change.

Analysis: `emitStableDatabaseSemconv()` returns a `static final boolean` through a small static method. The JVM can inline that read. Copying it into every request-span wrapper would add a field and a constructor assignment without evidence of a net cost reduction.

Upsides: Keeping the shared accessor avoids per-span state and keeps both Couchbase tracer versions consistent with other instrumentation.

Downsides: The source still contains a method call for each string attribute before JIT compilation.

threads.body: For non-`couchbase` / non-`couchbases` schemes that may still parse successfully, `CouchbaseServerTarget.defaultPort(scheme)` returns `-1`, which is then passed into `DbServerTarget.builder(-1)`. This can lead to incorrect port-rendering behavior (or potentially a malformed `DbServerTarget`) rather than cleanly returning `null`. Consider explicitly validating the parsed scheme before building the direct target (e.g., compute the default port and return `null` when it’s `< 0`).

replies.body:
No code change.

Analysis: Couchbase rejects arbitrary schemes before this builder runs. Current releases also accept `couchbase2` for Protostellar. With that supported scheme, `builder(-1)` drops a host with no port and correctly preserves an explicit port. Rejecting every scheme whose default port is unknown would drop valid `couchbase2` targets.

Upsides: Explicit Protostellar targets remain available, while malformed and incomplete targets still return `null`.

Downsides: A `couchbase2` target without an explicit port remains unavailable because this instrumentation does not know its default port.

Renaming the builder variable (and the corresponding `addSeed(DbServerTargetBuilder target, ...)` parameter) to something like `builder` would reduce cognitive overhead and make the code less error-prone.

replies.body:
No code change.

Analysis: `target` names the server target being assembled throughout this short method. The declared `DbServerTargetBuilder` type distinguishes the builder from the returned `CouchbaseServerTarget`. Renaming it is a preference and does not fix a defect.

Upsides: Keeping the name avoids a review-only rename with no behavior change.

Downsides: A reader may prefer the more mechanical name `builder`.

threads.body: [Testing] The cast is redundant: this assertion helper already accepts an `int` for an `AttributeKey<Long>`. Keeping `seedPort` as an `int` also preserves the mode-dependent expectation without extra conversion.

replies.body:
No code change.

Analysis: The nullable branch requires a boxed `Long`. Removing the cast selects `equalTo(AttributeKey<Long>, int)`, and Java then tries to unbox `null` in the false branch. `compileTestJava` reports `NullTernary` and `NullArgumentForNonNullParameter`. The cast makes the conditional type `Long` and preserves `null` as "attribute absent".

Upsides: Keeping the cast preserves the mode-dependent assertion and avoids an invalid null unboxing.

Downsides: The explicit cast can look redundant when the nullable branch is read in isolation.

threads.body: [General] This lookup cannot recover the target for supported Protostellar (`couchbase2://`) requests in current Couchbase 3.x. The SDK creates a `CoreProtostellar` (not `Core`) for that scheme, and `ProtostellarBaseRequest.context()` constructs its `RequestContext` with a null `Core`, so this always resolves to null and stable spans omit the configured `server.address`/`server.port` even though the parser intentionally accepts `couchbase2`. Please associate the target with a carrier available on the Protostellar request path and cover it in the latest-deps test.

replies.body:
Addressed in 21e9e0da4e48fca19949e48e840eec1a7589c852.

Analysis: `CoreProtostellar` receives the parsed connection string, but its request context has no `Core`. Store the parsed target on the `CoreProtostellar`, copy it to each `ProtostellarBaseRequest`, and read it from `RequestContext.request()`. Dynamically registered virtual fields keep these associations tied to the exact SDK carriers without raising the module's Couchbase 3.2 minimum version.

Upsides: Stable Protostellar spans report the configured server address and port. The latest-deps test covers the null-Core request path. Older Couchbase 3.2 clients remain supported.

Downsides: This adds two constructor advice hooks and dynamic virtual field lookup for SDK classes that do not exist in the minimum supported version.
